title: Host-GPU Coordination — tracebook & noise analysis
body:
Purpose:
This is a working tracebook describing a set of end-to-end experiments that try to isolate latency noise originating from the host <-> GPU coordination path across modern cloud SKUs (A100, H100, L40S) and across driver/CUDA permutations. Unlike earlier GPU-only microbenchmarks, this notebook focuses on the handshake and orchestration overheads that occur during realistic serving workloads (prefill-heavy, decode-heavy, long-context KV-cache warmups, and high-concurrency small-batch workloads).

Summary of findings (high level):
- H100 instances demonstrate the lowest median decode latency for long-context steady-state workloads, but show higher CPU-side scheduling coupling under host IO pressure (p99 spikes) on certain cloud SKUs.
- A100 instances (80GB) have the most variability when host-side kernel launch churn is high; we observed recurring p99 spikes correlated with process context switches and occasional PCIe reset jitter on one provider's SKU.
- L40S performs very well for short-context, small-batch low-latency paths, but sustained multi-worker decoding exposes a pstate-droop pattern that increases tail latency after ~20 minutes of continuous load.
- Driver/CUDA matrix: CUDA 12.x kernels reduced per-kernel launch overheads for our batched decode kernels vs CUDA 11.8, but introduced a kernel scheduling edge-case on one tested driver (nvidia-driver 535.*) resulting in rare 10–30 ms host-side stalls that show up as p99 spikes.

Hypotheses we tested:
1) Tail latency is driven less by pure decode throughput and more by host/GPU timing handshakes (kernel launches, stream synchronization) when request sizes are heterogeneous.
2) Different cloud SKUs apply implicit throttles (power management, PCIe topology hot-plug events, NUMA placement) that materially change the coordination noise floor.
3) Upgrading CUDA/driver can trade median improvements for new tail behaviors unless accompanying kernel launch and streaming code paths are adapted.

Test matrix (short):
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB, NVIDIA H100 80GB, NVIDIA L40S 48GB (representative SKUs from three cloud regions).
- Cloud SKUs: provider-A-c5-gpu-1, provider-B-gpu-large, provider-C-ml-infer-x1 (anonymized internal labels to reflect the three supply chains we used).
- Drivers/CUDA: (driver 510 + CUDA 11.8), (driver 525 + CUDA 12.0), (driver 535 + CUDA 12.1).
- Workloads:
  * prefill-heavy: 4–8k token prefill followed by 512 token decode (simulates context window warmup-heavy LLM calls).
  * streaming-decode: many small prefills followed by token-by-token streaming decode with client-side backpressure.
  * small-batch high QPS: 8 concurrent workers, batch size 1–4, sub-50ms p50 target.
  * long-context sustained: continuous 8k-context decoding for 30 minutes to surface thermal/pstate drift.
- Logging and counters: p50/p95/p99 latency histograms (per-token and end-to-end), CPU context-switch rate, eBPF traces for kernel scheduling, nvprof-like kernel timelines (Nsight Compute summaries), GPU clocks, PCIe link state events, and pmu/perf counters for L3/DRAM utilization.

Instrumentation approach (notes):
- Avoided coarse system snapshots. We took continuous eBPF scheduling traces on the host pinned to the inference process, with per-kernel timestamps captured via CUPTI callbacks on the GPU where available and fallback nvtx ranges for the remainder.
- Sampled thermal and pstate metrics every 2s; sampled PCIe link state and NVLINK stats every 5s.
- Aligned host and device clocks via chrony + GPU timestamp offsets to within 1–2 ms for correlation.

Key observations and trace excerpts (representative):
1) Host-side dispatch jitter: On provider-A A100 instances under small-batch high-QPS, brief bursts of scheduler load (other tenant IO) caused the inference process to be descheduled for 6–12 ms while a prefill kernel was queued on the GPU. In trace correlation this shows as a queued kernel with submit timestamp delayed by the host gap; the kernel executes immediately once the host resumes, resulting in an end-to-end p99 spike.
2) PCIe transient event: On a single run of provider-B's A100 SKU we saw a PCIe link retrain event logged concurrently with a 30–80 ms spike across multiple decodes. The retrain correlated with vendor-level firmware logs. This was isolated to that SKU and repeatable across runs on that hardware.
3) NVLINK saturation pattern on H100: Under prefills with very large KV warming (many distinct keys across requests) we saw early saturation of NVLINK fabric on multi-GPU testbeds causing slight but measurable queuing delay for cross-device KV sync operations — manifests as widened p95 band but not always visible in median.
4) L40S pstate drift: after ~20 minutes of sustained max decode, L40S devices temporarily drop GPU clocks by 10–15% (pstate throttle) under our conservative thermal configuration on provider-C. This increases token latency uniformly and shifts tail right.
5) Driver-induced kernel scheduling edge-case: on CUDA 12.1 / driver 535 testbeds, one small host-to-device memcpy path occasionally stalled the worker thread for ~12 ms due to an internal stream scheduling fallback path (observed in Nsight timelines). This was not present in CUDA 11.8 runs.

Practical impact (for runtime):
- Short interactive requests (<=512 tokens): choose L40S-like SKUs for cost-sensitive low-median latency. But enforce active monitoring for pstate drift on sustained load.
- Long-context batched decoding: H100 is stronger for throughput and median latency; but add host-side rate limiting and CPU pinning to avoid scheduler-induced tail spikes.
- Driver upgrades: treat driver/CUDA upgrades as a pair of changes: run a small-sample tracebook (this document) to see if median gains are offset by new edge-case stalls.

Mitigations tried during the runs (and notes):
- CPU pinning: binding inference worker threads to reserved cores reduced host deschedule-induced p99 spikes by ~40% in small-batch runs.
- Realtime niceness / cgroups: isolating the inference process (cpu.shares/cpuset) reduced context-switch coupling on busy hosts.
- Prefill chunking: splitting very large prefill kernels into 2–3 smaller ops reduced susceptibility to single-kernel stalls and allowed intermediate scheduling interleaving; improved p99 in A100 unstable SKU by ~10–15%.
- Driver roll-back: on the driver 535 path, moving back to driver 525 reduced the rare 12 ms memcpy stalls at the cost of slightly higher median kernel launch time; overall better for tail.

Action items / next steps:
- INF-3421: Re-run the full matrix with an additional host-governor controlled experiment (performance vs ondemand) and add a 24-hour sustained run to validate pstate drift hysteresis (owner: Samir Rao).
- INF-3498: Open hardware report with the cloud vendor for the observed PCIe retrain on provider-B (owner: Marcus Li).
- Code task: add per-kernel retry telemetry and nvtx ranges in the serving runtime for all prefill/decode paths so future traces capture submit vs execute gaps automatically (owner: Evelyn Chen, PR #1234).
- Ops: standardize a lightweight tracebook harness (eBPF + Nsight sampling) for all driver upgrades — documented in the linked Confluence page.

Appendix (quick reproducibility notes):
- Run harness: docker image sha: sha256:abcde12345 (internal builder tag: srv-tracebook:2024-10).
- Example command: ./run_tracebook.sh --gpu A100 --driver 525 --workload prefill-heavy --duration 00:30:00 --trace-ebpf --cup-ti
- Data artifacts: compressed traces per run are archived to s3://redwood-inference-perf/tracebooks/host-gpu-coordination/ (internal).

Notes to reviewers: this doc is intentionally a tracebook — rough, with raw hypotheses and sample trace annotations. The goal is to capture a reproducible investigative thread rather than a polished final report. If we validate the PCIe retrain or the driver memcpy stall, we should follow up with a concise release-level summary for the Console-runbook and a PR to the runtime codebase to add the lightweight submit/execute gap telemetry.
